Pheditor CVE-2026-48030 RCE: web shell_exec terminal handler with injected $dir metacharacters AIExploitation High
Hunts the Pheditor terminal handler command-injection chain by anchoring on the handler's literal shell_exec signature ('cd <dir> && <command> && echo \ ; pwd') and flagging cases where the 'cd' directory portion carries shell metacharacters (;, |, >, #, $(, backtick). This is the exact RCE path in pheditor.php lines 554-586 where $dir bypasses the TERMINAL_COMMANDS whitelist. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact vulnerable code (pheditor.php L586): every terminal invocation produces 'cd <dir> && <command> && echo \ ; pwd', so the literal 'echo \ ; pwd' tail scopes precisely to Pheditor, and metacharacters in the captured cd-directory portion are the injection itself (the whitelist only guards $command). Behaviour-only detection; no network IOCs in the advisory to validate. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843 • https://github.com/advisories?query=severity%3Acritical
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator using the Pheditor terminal legitimately with a path that genuinely contains a '#' anchor or '$' (rare for filesystem paths)
  • Security team running the published PoC against an authorized test/staging instance
  • Automated vulnerability scanner (Burp/Nuclei) replaying the CVE-2026-48030 check in a sanctioned pen-test window
  • A developer's own shell script that coincidentally ends commands with 'echo \ ; pwd' (extremely rare; the backslash-space form is idiosyncratic to Pheditor)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("nuclei","sqlmap","burp") and DeviceName has_any ("test","staging","lab"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and DirPart; confirm a real metacharacter (;, |, >, $( , backtick, #) sits inside the 'cd' portion and identify the injected payload (curl/echo/webshell write). Check the parent (php-fpm/apache2) and the source IP from the web tier. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the offending sh/child processes, and rotate the Pheditor admin credential; remove terminal permission and patch to a fixed build (escapeshellarg on $dir). 3) HUNT: Pivot on UC2/UC3 for any .php webshell dropped under the webroot and any outbound curl/wget from the web user; review web access logs for repeated POSTs to pheditor.php with action=terminal.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine contains @"echo \ ; pwd"   // pheditor terminal handler signature: shell_exec(... ' && echo \ ; pwd')
| extend DirPart = extract(@"cd (.+?) && ", 1, ProcessCommandLine)   // the unsanitised $dir portion before the appended command
| where isnotempty(DirPart)
| where DirPart matches regex @"[;|<>#\x60]|\$\("   // injected shell metacharacters that bypass the $command whitelist
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessCommandLine, DirPart, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash") or ActingProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine contains @"echo \ ; pwd"   // pheditor terminal handler signature
| extend DirPart = extract(@"cd (.+?) && ", 1, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(DirPart)
| where DirPart matches regex @"[;|<>#\x60]|\$\("   // injected metacharacters in the $dir parameter
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, DirPart
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Pheditor CVE-2026-48030 Command Injection via Terminal Handler dir Parameter
id: 6f1c2a9e-3d84-4b27-9a1e-2c7f0b5d8e41
description: Detects exploitation of CVE-2026-48030 where shell metacharacters injected into the Pheditor terminal handler's dir parameter are passed to shell_exec, identified by the handler's literal 'echo \ ; pwd' signature plus metacharacters in the cd-directory portion.

  injection:
    CommandLine|re: 'cd [^&]*[;|<>#`$]'
  condition: signature and injection
falsepositives:

level: high

| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash)$/i

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Pheditor webshell drop: PHP file written to webroot by Pheditor terminal shell_exec AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-exploitation step from the CVE-2026-48030 PoC where the injected dir command writes a PHP webshell into the webroot (e.g. /var/www/html/shell.php). Ties the .php file creation to the Pheditor handler by requiring the writing process command line to carry the handler's 'echo \ ; pwd' signature, making it laser-specific to this CVE rather than generic file-drop noise. Rationale: Mirrors the PoC step 5 verbatim ('echo \'<?php system($_GET[\"c\"]);?>\' > /var/www/html/shell.php'); requiring the writer's command line to contain the 'echo \ ; pwd' handler signature ties the .php drop directly to the vulnerable Pheditor handler, eliminating generic webroot-write FPs. The Defender/Sentinel variants carry that signature; the CIM/Sigma/Falcon variants fall back to path+extension+web-writer because those schemas don't expose the spawning shell's full command line on the file event. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Composer / Packagist dependency install dropping PHP files into the webroot
  • WordPress/Drupal/Laravel plugin or theme installation writing .php into web directories
  • CI/CD deploy pipeline rsync/cp of application PHP into /var/www
  • Admin manually editing/creating a PHP file via the (legitimate) Pheditor save function rather than the terminal
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("composer","php","git","rsync","cp","tar","unzip") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains @"echo \ ; pwd"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the newly written .php file (FolderPath + FileName); confirm it contains a webshell pattern (system/exec/passthru/eval on $_GET/$_POST) and capture the SHA256. 2) CONTAIN: Quarantine/delete the file, isolate the host, block the web user from spawning shells, and reset Pheditor admin credentials; patch to the fixed Pheditor build. 3) HUNT: Search web access logs for GET requests to the dropped file name (e.g. shell.php?c=), review all .php files in the webroot modified in the same window, and pivot to UC1 for the injecting terminal command and UC3 for outbound callbacks.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/var/www/","/www/","/usr/share/nginx/","/srv/www/")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains @"echo \ ; pwd"   // write originated from the pheditor terminal shell_exec chain
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/var/www/","/www/","/usr/share/nginx/","/srv/www/")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine contains @"echo \ ; pwd"   // write originated from the pheditor terminal shell_exec chain
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Pheditor post-exploitation: web server user spawns curl/wget egress via injected dir command AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-48030 PoC's network egress step where the injected dir command runs curl/wget under the web server context (the PoC uses 'curl -s https://ifconfig.me' for IP discovery and curl to attacker.com). Flags network/download tools spawned by a shell or PHP/web-server parent reaching a public address — the data-discovery and download stage of the RCE. Rationale: Maps the PoC steps 4 (curl -s https://ifconfig.me for public-IP discovery) and the curl attacker.com exfil example: a network/download tool spawned by a shell or PHP/web-server parent under the web user is the egress fingerprint of the RCE. Marked hunting/medium because some PHP apps legitimately invoke curl — pair with UC1/UC2 hits on the same host to confirm. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A PHP application legitimately shelling out to curl/wget for API callbacks, package downloads, or remote health checks
  • Cron jobs running as the web user that fetch remote files
  • Monitoring/agent scripts under the web account hitting external endpoints
  • Composer or deploy hooks invoking curl during application updates
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("packagist.org","composer","api.github.com") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Capture the curl/wget command line and the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl; determine whether the destination is a known-good app dependency or an unfamiliar/attacker host (e.g. ifconfig.me or a raw IP). Confirm the parent is a shell rather than the application binary. 2) CONTAIN: If destination is suspicious, block it at the egress proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and kill the process tree. 3) HUNT: Correlate to UC1 (injecting terminal command) and UC2 (webshell drop) on the same host within the window, review what was downloaded/uploaded, and check the webroot for new files created right after the connection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","php-fpm","php","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","/nc","ncat")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","php-fpm","php","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AWS CloudTrail blinded: StopLogging / DeleteTrail / UpdateTrail / PutEventSelectors AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the article's Technique 1 (Stop Logging) and the AWS analog of Technique 3 (Delete Log Router) — an identity invoking the CloudTrail management APIs that suspend or reconfigure a trail, creating an immediate visibility gap before the rest of an intrusion. Targets cloudtrail.amazonaws.com control-plane events, which are exceptionally rare outside change-management. Rationale: Uses the article's explicitly named cloudtrail:StopLogging / stop-logging API plus the corroborated trail-tamper set (DeleteTrail/UpdateTrail/PutEventSelectors) confirmed by MITRE T1562.008 and Stratus Red Team as the AWS 'delete log router' analog. These are management-plane events with near-zero legitimate user-space volume. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/ • https://stratus-red-team.cloud/attack-techniques/AWS/aws.defense-evasion.cloudtrail-stop/ • https://aws-samples.github.io/threat-technique-catalog-for-aws/Techniques/T1562.008.html
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Terraform/CloudFormation pipeline updating a trail's event selectors during a planned deploy
  • Account/region decommissioning by cloud platform team removing trails
  • Cost-optimization work reducing data-event selectors via PutEventSelectors
  • Migration from per-account trails to an Organization trail (DeleteTrail on old trails)
  • Break-glass automation role rotating trail config
Suppression filter
and userIdentity.arn not like /(?i)(terraform|cloudformation|deploy|cicd|automation)/
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the caller (userIdentity.arn/type) and sourceIPAddress; confirm whether the principal is a known IaC/automation role and whether a change ticket exists for this trail name. Step 2 — Contain: if unauthorized, re-enable the trail (StartLogging) or recreate it, and immediately revoke/quarantine the offending principal's session and access keys via SCP/permission boundary. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same principal/IP for activity in the visibility gap window — IAM changes, S3 access, AssumeRole chains, and the S3 log-bucket deletion detection (UC2). Verify Organization-trail coverage was not also impacted.
title: AWS CloudTrail Logging Disabled or Trail Tampered
id: 6f0e2b1a-3c4d-4e5f-9a8b-1c2d3e4f5a6b
description: Detects CloudTrail management API calls that stop, delete or reconfigure a trail (StopLogging/DeleteTrail/UpdateTrail/PutEventSelectors), blinding cloud visibility.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cloud-logging-defense-evasion/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1562.008
logsource:
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    eventSource: cloudtrail.amazonaws.com
    eventName:
      - StopLogging
      - DeleteTrail
      - UpdateTrail
      - PutEventSelectors
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Authorized infrastructure-as-code changes to trail configuration
  - Decommissioning of an account or region
level: high
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:(StopLogging OR DeleteTrail OR UpdateTrail OR PutEventSelectors) @evt.outcome:success
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.type, sourceIPAddress, requestParameters.name, awsRegion
| filter eventSource = "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["StopLogging", "DeleteTrail", "UpdateTrail", "PutEventSelectors"]
      and not isPresent(errorCode)
| sort @timestamp desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where (All_Changes.command IN ("StopLogging","DeleteTrail","UpdateTrail","PutEventSelectors")) AND All_Changes.status="success" by All_Changes.user All_Changes.command All_Changes.object All_Changes.src All_Changes.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where (All_Changes.command IN ("StopLogging","DeleteTrail","UpdateTrail","PutEventSelectors")) AND All_Changes.status="success" by All_Changes.user All_Changes.command All_Changes.object All_Changes.src All_Changes.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
AWS S3 deletion of CloudTrail log-destination bucket/objects AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the article's Technique 2 (Delete Log Storage Destination) in AWS — an identity calling DeleteBucket / DeleteObject(s) against the S3 bucket that stores CloudTrail logs, destroying forensic evidence. Scopes to buckets whose names indicate a logging/audit role to separate this from routine object lifecycle. Rationale: Built on the article's named s3:DeleteBucket + s3:DeleteObject permissions / delete-bucket API for emptying and removing the log store. S3 bucket names are forced lowercase by AWS, so the logging/audit/trail name scope is reliable and removes generic object-deletion noise, keeping this aimed at the forensic-evidence-destruction step. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/ • https://aws-samples.github.io/threat-technique-catalog-for-aws/Techniques/T1562.008.html
ATT&CKT1562.008 T1485
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled lifecycle job purging expired CloudTrail logs from an archive bucket
  • Platform team decommissioning a legacy logging account/bucket
  • Replatforming logs from S3 to CloudTrail Lake and tearing down the old bucket
  • Cost-cleanup deleting an unused duplicate log bucket
  • Backup/DR tooling rotating object versions in a log bucket
Suppression filter
and userIdentity.arn not like /(?i)(lifecycle|backup|terraform|cloudformation|automation)/
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the bucketName is an active CloudTrail/log destination (cross-check trail S3BucketName config) and whether the deleting principal is an authorized lifecycle/automation role with a change record. Step 2 — Contain: if unauthorized, enable S3 Object Lock / versioning recovery, restore from replication/backup, and revoke the principal's credentials; apply a bucket policy + SCP denying delete on logging buckets. Step 3 — Hunt: correlate with UC1 (trail StopLogging) by the same principal/IP, review what occurred in the resulting log gap, and check for KMS key disablement or denial affecting log readability.

GCP Cloud Logging tampering: sink disabled/deleted or log bucket deleted AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the article's Technique 1 & 2 in Google Cloud — UpdateSink (setting disabled=true), DeleteSink, and log-bucket deletion via the Cloud Logging ConfigServiceV2 admin APIs, which stop or destroy the log-routing/storage pipeline. Targets Admin Activity audit logs where these control-plane methods appear. Rationale: Uses the article's named logging.sinks.update (sink disabled=true) and logging.buckets.delete actions, mapped to the corroborated method names google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink/DeleteSink/DeleteBucket (Elastic and Datadog prebuilt rules confirm these). These admin-activity methods are low-volume and tie directly to the GCP defense-evasion path. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/security/current/gcp-logging-sink-deletion.html • https://docs.datadoghq.com/security/default_rules/google-cloud-logging-sink-modified/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Logging admin editing a sink's inclusion filter (benign UpdateSink)
  • Platform team retiring an unused export sink (DeleteSink)
  • Terraform google_logging_project_sink lifecycle apply
  • Decommissioning a log bucket past its retention need
  • Migration of log routing between destinations during re-architecture
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify principalEmail and callerIp from the audit record; for UpdateSink inspect protoPayload.request to confirm whether disabled was set true vs a benign filter edit, and check for an approved change. Step 2 — Contain: if unauthorized, re-enable/recreate the sink or restore the log bucket (note: deleted log buckets sit in DELETE_REQUESTED for 7 days and can be undeleted), and revoke the principal's IAM roles/keys. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same principal for IAM SetIamPolicy changes, service-account key creation, and storage access during the logging gap; verify org-level sinks remained intact.
title: GCP Cloud Logging Sink or Bucket Tampering

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where (All_Changes.command IN ("google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink","google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteSink","google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteBucket")) AND All_Changes.status="success" by All_Changes.user All_Changes.command All_Changes.object All_Changes.src | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

BEAM VM (beam.smp) spawns shell/recon process — phoenix_storybook HEEx RCE payload (CVE-2026-8467) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation execution stage of CVE-2026-8467, where the injected inline HEEx Elixir expression (e.g. System.cmd/2) causes the Erlang VM to spawn an OS command. A production Phoenix/BEAM process spawning sh/bash/whoami/curl is highly abnormal and indicates the storybook playground RCE fired. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploitation primitive — an injected inline Elixir expression (System.cmd/2) evaluated by EEx.compile_string + Code.eval_quoted_with_env — which manifests as the BEAM VM (beam.smp / erl_child_setup) spawning a shell or recon binary. Cross-checked against cna.erlef.org and sentinelone.com confirming unauthenticated server-side code execution. Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: the listed Datadog Linux sources (auditd EXECVE) carry no parent-process field to express the beam.smp parent link, and this is not AWS telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://cna.erlef.org/cves/CVE-2026-8467.html • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-8467/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Elixir release entrypoint/healthcheck legitimately invoking System.cmd("sh", ...) or :os.cmd for ops tasks
  • Mix tasks or deployment hooks shelling out to curl/wget during boot
  • Application code that legitimately calls uname/hostname for telemetry/metrics
  • Sidecar/agent integrations where the app shells to base64 or chmod on startup
  • Library NIF builds (make) at app startup invoking sh
Suppression filter
| where not(ChildCmd has_any ("mix ","/app/bin/","releases/","_build/")) // drop release-boot / mix-task shellouts
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ChildCmd/CommandLine of the beam.smp-spawned process and the source host; benign ops calls look static and recurring, RCE looks like ad-hoc recon (whoami;id;uname) or egress (curl to unknown IP). Correlate the timestamp with inbound requests to /storybook and the deployed phoenix_storybook version (must be >=0.5.0 <1.1.0). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block egress to any IP the spawned process contacted, and take the storybook route offline (remove live_storybook mount or gate it behind auth) — upgrade to phoenix_storybook 1.1.0. 3) Hunt: search the same host for follow-on shells, dropped files in /tmp, new cron/systemd persistence, and outbound C2 from beam.smp; review all source IPs that hit /storybook in the prior 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("beam.smp","erl_child_setup","erlexec","beam")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","whoami","id","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","ruby","base64","chmod")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","erl_child_setup","erlexec")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","whoami","/id","uname","hostname","curl","wget","/nc","ncat","python","perl","base64","chmod")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

External access to phoenix_storybook playground route /storybook (CVE-2026-8467 attack surface) AIDelivery Low
Surfaces inbound HTTP/WebSocket access from public (non-internal) source IPs to the phoenix_storybook default mount path /storybook, which exposes the unauthenticated playground that drives CVE-2026-8467. A publicly reachable storybook is the precondition for the pre-auth RCE. Rationale: Pivots on the product's documented default mount path /storybook (confirmed via hexdocs.pm) restricted to external (non-RFC1918) source IPs — matching the advisory's stated risk of a publicly deployed storybook being unauthenticated-RCE-able. Low confidence / hunting because the injection payload itself rides in the LiveView WebSocket frame (psb-assign event), not the URL, so this surfaces attack-surface exposure rather than confirmed exploitation. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: inbound web-path telemetry does not live in endpoint EDR or AWS CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://hexdocs.pm/phoenix_storybook/PhoenixStorybook.html • https://cna.erlef.org/cves/CVE-2026-8467.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal developers/designers browsing the storybook from VPN-egress or cloud NAT IPs that appear non-private
  • Legitimate public storybook used as a living style-guide/documentation site
  • Uptime monitors or synthetic checks hitting /storybook
  • Security scanners / ASM tooling crawling the app surface
  • CDN or load-balancer health probes rewritten to external source IPs
Suppression filter
| where not(RequestClientApplication has_any ("Pingdom","UptimeRobot","StatusCake","Datadog")) // drop known synthetic monitors
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether /storybook is intentionally public and what phoenix_storybook version is deployed (vulnerable: >=0.5.0 <1.1.0); profile the external source IPs and user-agents — automation/scanner UAs hitting the playground are higher priority. 2) Contain: if unintended, gate the live_storybook route behind an auth Plug pipeline or remove it in production, and upgrade to 1.1.0. 3) Hunt: for any flagged source IP, pivot to UC1 (beam.smp spawning shells) on the web host around the same window, and review LiveView WebSocket connections (/live/websocket) from that IP.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/storybook"
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| summarize Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(RequestURL, 25), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DeviceProduct, RequestClientApplication
| order by Requests desc

Elixir app-log errors from phoenix_storybook HEEx eval (component_renderer / Code.eval_quoted) — CVE-2026-8467 exploitation attempts AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Phoenix/Elixir application error logs that reference the vulnerable phoenix_storybook code path (component_renderer / attributes_markup / Code.eval_quoted_with_env / EEx CompileError). The advisory notes the injected expression evaluates even when rendering errors, so both failed and successful injection attempts emit these traces. Rationale: Built from the exact source-file and function names disclosed in the advisory — component_renderer.ex / ComponentRenderer.attributes_markup/1 / EEx.compile_string / Code.eval_quoted_with_env/3 — which a probe of the unsanitized HEEx attribute path surfaces in the BEAM error log even when the render fails. Medium confidence because these strings co-occurring is exploitation-specific to the vulnerable code path. Splunk left non-tstats (raw search) because Elixir application logs have no CIM datamodel mapping; Defender/Falcon empty as BEAM app logs are not EDR/script-scan telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-55hg-8qxv-qj4p • https://cna.erlef.org/cves/CVE-2026-8467.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer testing of storybook components in a non-prod environment generating render/compile errors
  • Benign EEx CompileError from unrelated template authoring that happens to log near storybook modules
  • Application crash-dumps that enumerate the full dependency tree including PhoenixStorybook without an actual injection
  • Log-replay or SIEM re-ingestion duplicating historical error traces
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full SyslogMessage stack trace — a real injection shows attacker-controlled attribute content (stray closing-quote breakout, an inline {expr}) inside the eval/compile error; note the deployed phoenix_storybook version. 2) Contain: if exploitation is evident, isolate the host, pull the storybook route / upgrade to 1.1.0, and rotate any secrets reachable by the server process (the eval runs with full Kernel access). 3) Hunt: correlate the host+window with UC1 (beam.smp spawning shells) and UC2 (external /storybook hits) to confirm the full chain, and grep app logs for repeated breakout attempts from the same session.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "PhoenixStorybook" or SyslogMessage has "component_renderer" or SyslogMessage has "attributes_markup"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("EEx", "Code.eval_quoted", "eval_quoted_with_env", "CompileError", "SyntaxError")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog ("PhoenixStorybook" OR "component_renderer" OR "attributes_markup") AND ("EEx" OR "Code.eval_quoted" OR "eval_quoted_with_env" OR "CompileError")

Bun runtime executed from temp dir running _index.js payload (Hades Campaign) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Hades/Miasma supply-chain second stage: the Python import hook downloads a standalone Bun runtime into a temp 'b' directory and runs the malicious _index.js bundle via `bun run _index.js`. This is the article's most specific execution artifact and is unusual in any normal developer/CI environment. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim execution string `bun run _index.js` plus the standalone `bun` binary name from the deobfuscated import hook — the binary+args combination has no legitimate occurrence in normal environments. Detections built from article strings; no external IOC bundle located for this 2026 campaign.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.006 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately running a project whose entry bundle is genuinely named _index.js via `bun run`
  • CI pipeline that builds with Bun and has a script step named 'run' touching an _index.js
  • Local benchmarking/testing of the Bun runtime by an engineer evaluating it
  • Monorepo tooling that invokes `bun run` against framework-generated _index.js artifacts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","pip","sh","bash") or FolderPath has "/b/bun"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree — confirm the parent is a python/python3 interpreter importing a package (site-packages path) and that the bun binary lives under a temp '/b/' directory rather than a project node_modules. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, kill the bun process, and remove /tmp/b/bun, /tmp/b.zip and the /tmp/.bun_ran flag file; rotate any cloud/CI secrets exposed to that runner. 3) Hunt: pivot on the package that triggered the import (ensmallen 0.8.101, embiggen 0.11.97, gpsea 0.9.14, pyphetools 0.9.120, nhmpy 2.4.7, ppkt2synergy 0.1.1, mflux-streamlit 0.0.3/0.0.4) across all hosts and check for outbound GitHub exfil.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "run" and ProcessCommandLine has "_index.js"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "bun"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "run" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "_index.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scripting interpreter downloads Bun v1.3.14 runtime from oven-sh GitHub releases AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Hades delivery step where the Python hook calls urlretrieve to pull the pinned Bun runtime ZIP (bun-v1.3.14) from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases. The high-fidelity signal is a Python/Node interpreter (not a browser or package manager) fetching the platform-specific bun ZIP to bootstrap an out-of-band JS engine. Rationale: Uses the exact pinned download path from the deobfuscated hook — `github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.14/bun-{os}-{arch}.zip` — combined with a scripting-interpreter initiating process, which distinguishes malware bootstrap from a developer's browser download. Medium confidence because legitimate Bun adoption exists; pin on the interpreter parent + exact version path.
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CI job legitimately installing/upgrading Bun v1.3.14 via a script
  • Internal mirror/proxy prefetching GitHub release assets
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation pulling Bun toolchain
  • DevContainer or Docker build step that fetches Bun for a real project
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","curl","wget")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting process is a Python interpreter executing inside a freshly imported package (not an intentional `bun upgrade`/devcontainer build); check for a co-occurring /tmp/.bun_ran write within seconds. 2) Contain: block the host's egress, quarantine the downloaded ZIP and extracted bun binary, and rotate CI/cloud tokens reachable from the host. 3) Hunt: search for subsequent `bun run _index.js` execution and outbound connections to GitHub for credential exfiltration on the same and peer runners.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","node","bun")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oven-sh/bun","bun-v1.3.14","bun-linux-","bun-darwin-","bun-windows-")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession

| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(github\.com|objects\.githubusercontent\.com|release-assets\.githubusercontent\.com)$/i

Hades import-hook payload artifacts dropped (_index.js, _hooks.py, _runtime.bin, .bun_ran, b.zip) AIInstallation High
Hunts file creation of the named Hades/Miasma payload and persistence artifacts: _hooks.py / _runtime.bin / modified __init__.py committed into a repo (the gpt-pilot compromise), plus the runtime drops _index.js, b.zip and the /tmp/.bun_ran once-per-boot flag. Tight filename list keyed to scripting-interpreter writers makes this article-specific. Rationale: Filenames are taken verbatim from the article's code blocks and compromise table (_hooks.py, _runtime.bin added alongside a modified __init__.py; runtime drops _index.js, b.zip, and the /tmp/.bun_ran flag). These names are attacker-fixed so a single casing suffices and FP risk is low when paired with an interpreter/git writer.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006 T1027

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A real project that legitimately ships a file named _index.js or _hooks.py in source control
  • Test fixtures or scaffolding tools generating b.zip archives
  • A developer manually creating a dotfile coincidentally named .bun_ran
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a monitored sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/site-packages/","/dist-packages/") and FileName == "_index.js" and InitiatingProcessFileName has "pip")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the writing process — confirm it is a Python import (site-packages parent) or a git checkout pulling a backdoored commit, and inspect __init__.py for the obfuscated single-line exec import hook. 2) Contain: delete the dropped artifacts, kill any spawned bun process, isolate the host, and revoke secrets the host could reach. 3) Hunt: diff the offending repo for a force-pushed 'Revert' commit (e.g. malicious SHA 065ee8eb vs clean 566fbb12) and sweep peers for the same package versions and /tmp/.bun_ran flag.

CI runner secret theft via /proc/<pid>/mem read of Runner.Worker (Miasma memory scraper) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Miasma Linux memory-scraping technique carried into the Hades Campaign: a scripting interpreter walks /proc/<pid>/maps and reads /proc/<pid>/mem of the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process to scrape plaintext secrets from memory. Targets the proc-filesystem credential access primitive directly. Rationale: Targets the article's named credential-access primitive — reading /proc/<pid>/mem of Runner.Worker to scrape plaintext secrets — anchored on the /proc/<pid>/mem path and a scripting-interpreter opener. Defender Advanced Hunting has no /proc read telemetry, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; detection is expressed on Falcon FileOpenInfo and Linux auditd/Syslog where the path is observable.
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Debuggers (gdb, lldb) or profilers legitimately reading /proc/<pid>/mem
  • Crash-dump/coredump tooling (e.g. core_pattern handlers, gcore)
  • Security/EDR agents or memory-forensics tools sampling process memory
  • Container runtime introspection reading process maps on a CI host
Suppression filter
| ContextImageFileName!=/(gdb|lldb|gcore|crash|systemd-coredump|strace)/i
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the reader process and the target PID — confirm the target is Runner.Worker (or another secret-bearing process) and that the reader is an unexpected python/bun spawned from a package import, not gdb/coredump tooling. 2) Contain: kill the reader, isolate the runner, and immediately rotate every secret/token that runner had access to (cloud keys, GH tokens, registry creds). 3) Hunt: correlate with the bun bootstrap (`bun run _index.js`), /tmp/.bun_ran flag, and outbound GitHub exfil; expand to macOS runners for task_for_pid-based scraping by the same package set.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/proc/" and SyslogMessage has "/mem"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("python","bun","Runner.Worker")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Miasma Worm Hits Microsoft Again: Azure Functions Action and 72 Other Repositories Disabled After Supply Chain Attack Targeting AI Coding Agents

StepSecurity
2026-06-09 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On June 5, 2026, the Miasma worm campaign reached Microsoft's Azure GitHub organizations. GitHub disabled 73 repositories across four Microsoft GitHub organizations after a malicious commit was pushed to the Azure/durabletask repository using a previously compromised contributor account. The attack planted configuration files that execute a credential-harvesting payload when a developer opens the repository in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or VS Code.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Suspicious commit pattern: '[skip ci]' with backdated timestamp adding only IDE config files · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] node.exe spawned by Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini executing .github/setup.js · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Miasma Worm Hits Microsoft Again: Azure Functions Action and 72 Other Repositori
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious AI coding-agent hook configs written to repo (.claude/.gemini/.cursor/.vscode) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound DNS / HTTP to Miasma C2 (git-service.com / m-kosche.com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Malicious AI coding-agent hook configs written to repo (.claude/.gemini/.cursor/.vscode) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma worm's signature artifact: simultaneous creation of SessionStart hooks and folderOpen tasks in .claude/settings.json, .gemini/settings.json, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, and .vscode/tasks.json — all pointing at node .github/setup.js. This is the precise file-set planted in the June 5 2026 Azure/durabletask commit 5f456b8. Rationale: The five planted-file paths are verbatim from the article's 'Five Planted Files, Four Attack Vectors' section. Requiring >=2 co-occurrence per host suppresses single legitimate .vscode/tasks.json edits while keeping near-zero FP on the Miasma file-set. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/ • https://github.com/step-security/supply-chain-firewall
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer scaffolding a new repo with VS Code tasks.json AND committing a .vscode workspace file at the same time
  • Engineering platform team rolling out a corporate .cursor/rules/ template across repos
  • Repo containing legitimate .github/setup.js for project bootstrapping (rare; size + obfuscation differentiates)
  • Renovate/Dependabot edits to .vscode/tasks.json without other paired files (will not trigger >=2 threshold)
  • Developer copying a template repo locally that legitimately includes both .claude and .vscode dirs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","Code.exe","Cursor.exe") and array_length(ArtifactsSeen) == 1 and ArtifactsSeen has "vscode-folderopen")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess (typically git.exe / Code.exe checkout) and inspect the .github/setup.js size and entropy; the Miasma payload is exactly 4,643,745 bytes single-line obfuscated JS. Pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for any node.exe child within 60s. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, kill any node setup.js process tree, force-revoke the developer's GitHub PAT / OAuth tokens, cloud CLI tokens (aws, az, gcloud), and rotate any .npmrc / .pypirc / kubeconfig secrets that the harvester targets. Step 3 — Hunt: search the org for any repo containing the five planted paths via GitHub code-search API; check for outbound DNS to check.git-service.com / t.m-kosche.com / git-service.com from any developer endpoint in the past 30 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
| extend Artifact = case(
    FolderPath has @"\.claude\settings.json", "claude-hook",
    FolderPath has @"\.gemini\settings.json", "gemini-hook",
    FolderPath has @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", "cursor-prompt-injection",
    FolderPath has @"\.vscode\tasks.json", "vscode-folderopen",
    FolderPath has @"\.github\setup.js", "miasma-payload", "other")
| summarize ArtifactsSeen = make_set(Artifact), Paths = make_set(FolderPath), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where array_length(ArtifactsSeen) >= 2  // co-occurrence of >=2 of the 5 planted files
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
| extend Artifact = case(
    TargetFilePath has @"\.claude\settings.json", "claude-hook",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.gemini\settings.json", "gemini-hook",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", "cursor-prompt-injection",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.vscode\tasks.json", "vscode-folderopen",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.github\setup.js", "miasma-payload", "other")
| summarize ArtifactsSeen = make_set(Artifact), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| where array_length(ArtifactsSeen) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Miasma Worm AI-Agent Hook Config Planted
id: 8a2a4e0f-3d9c-4b7d-9b4f-1d2e7c61a210
description: Detects creation of SessionStart hooks / folderOpen tasks / Cursor prompt-injection rules that the Miasma worm plants in compromised repos to auto-execute node .github/setup.js when a developer opens the project in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or VS Code.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-worm-hits-microsoft-again-azure-functions-action-and-72-other-repositories-disabled-after-supply-chain-attack-targeting-ai-coding-agents
author: SOC Detection Engineering

  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1546

    TargetFilename|endswith:

      - '\.vscode\tasks.json'
      - '\.github\setup.js'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\.claude\\settings.json OR *\\.gemini\\settings.json OR *\\.cursor\\rules\\setup.mdc OR *\\.vscode\\tasks.json OR *\\.github\\setup.js))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\\.(claude|gemini)\\\\settings\.json$|\\\.cursor\\\\rules\\\\setup\.mdc$|\\\.vscode\\\\tasks\.json$|\\\.github\\\\setup\.js$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=[count(), collect(TargetFileName)])
| _count >= 2

node.exe spawned by Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini executing .github/setup.js AIExploitation High
Hunts the Miasma worm's automatic execution chain: VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, or Gemini CLI launching node.exe with .github/setup.js as the script argument. This is the runtime detonation produced when a developer simply opens a repo containing the planted hook configs. Rationale: Article quotes the exact command 'node .github/setup.js' invoked by all four planted configs (Claude SessionStart, Gemini SessionStart, Cursor prompt injection, VS Code folderOpen task). Anchoring on parent IDE + node.exe + setup.js path is high-fidelity because legitimate projects rarely store bootstrap scripts under .github/. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/ • https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/tasks#_run-behavior
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer with a legitimate project-bootstrap node script genuinely under .github/setup.js
  • Internal devtools team running .github/setup.js via VS Code task as a sanctioned scaffold
  • CI runner image with cached IDE binaries executing setup scripts during build
  • Repo template repos where setup.js is an intentional installer
  • Security researcher analysing the Miasma sample in a sandbox (whitelist sandbox host IDs)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has "sandbox" or DeviceName has "malware-lab")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: hash the setup.js (expect 4,643,745 bytes / SHA256 mismatch to any known-good repo) and capture the first 1 KB of the single-line obfuscated JS for IR. Pull network egress from the node.exe PID. Step 2 — Contain: kill the node process tree, isolate the host, and revoke developer-context credentials — GitHub PAT/OAuth, AWS/Azure/GCP CLI tokens, kubeconfig, NPM/PyPI tokens, SSH keys (article confirms harvester targets AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes + 90+ dev tool configs). Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate all repos cloned on the host in the past 30 days and check each working tree for the five planted paths; sweep the org's GitHub for commits with message 'Switched DataConverter to OrchestrationContext [skip ci]' or backdated commits to 2020-03-09.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@".github\setup.js", ".github/setup.js")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","claude.exe","claude-code.exe","gemini.exe","node.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@".github\setup.js", ".github/setup.js")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","claude.exe","claude-code.exe","gemini.exe","node.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound DNS / HTTP to Miasma C2 (git-service.com / m-kosche.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts resolution or connection to the Miasma worm's credential-exfiltration infrastructure: check.git-service.com, git-service.com, and t.m-kosche.com. These domains receive harvested AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes/dev-tool secrets from the planted payload. Rationale: Three domains are explicitly listed in the article's pre-extracted IOCs (check.git-service.com, t.m-kosche.com, git-service.com). Article says credential-harvesting payload exfiltrates AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes/dev-tool secrets, so DNS+network egress to these domains is high-fidelity C2. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-worm-hits-microsoft-again-azure-functions-action-and-72-other-repositories-disabled-after-supply-chain-attack-targeting-ai-coding-agents
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate enterprise self-hosted Git on a sub-domain that coincidentally matches *git-service.com (rare; whitelist by exact FQDN)
  • Threat-intel feed fetcher / sandbox detonation system (whitelist sandbox host IDs)
  • Security researcher visiting the domain for reverse-engineering
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ infrastructure resolving the indicator (whitelist sinkhole resolver IP)
  • Browsing to the StepSecurity blog post itself (won't hit subdomains directly)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sinkhole","sandbox","ti-fetcher"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the initiating process and user; if InitiatingProcessFileName is node.exe, immediately pivot to its command line for .github/setup.js. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, block the three domains at the corporate resolver and egress proxy, and treat all credentials accessible from the user/host context as compromised — rotate cloud tokens, GitHub PATs, NPM/PyPI/Cargo registry tokens, kubeconfig, SSH keys. Step 3 — Hunt: 30-day lookback across the entire fleet for any resolution of git-service.com or m-kosche.com; correlate hits with file-creation of .github/setup.js or the four IDE hook configs to find latent infections.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com") or RemoteUrl in~ ("check.git-service.com","t.m-kosche.com","git-service.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Name has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP, Domain = Name, QueryType = QueryTypeName, Result),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host = SrcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, Domain = DnsQuery, QueryType = DnsQueryTypeName, Result = DnsResponseCodeName),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationDnsDomain has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com") or RequestURL has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host = SourceHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, Domain = coalesce(DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL), QueryType = "proxy", Result = DeviceAction)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suspicious commit pattern: '[skip ci]' with backdated timestamp adding only IDE config files AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Miasma commit fingerprint: a single push where 5 files added / 0 source files modified, commit message ends with '[skip ci]', author date backdated to a pre-2024 timestamp, and the added paths include AI-agent config dirs. Detects via GitHub Audit Log shipped to Sentinel/Defender via CloudAppEvents or to Datadog via the GitHub integration. Rationale: Article details the exact commit fingerprint: commit 5f456b8 with message 'Switched DataConverter to OrchestrationContext [skip ci]', 5 files added / 0 source files modified, backdated to 2020-03-09T15:59:47Z (six years before push). The conjunction of [skip ci] + backdated author date + added IDE-config paths is the Miasma operator signature. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/admin/monitoring-activity-in-your-enterprise/reviewing-audit-logs-for-your-enterprise
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate maintainer importing an old Git history with [skip ci] in a merge commit
  • Repository migration from another VCS preserving original author dates pre-2024
  • CI maintenance commit adding .vscode/tasks.json with [skip ci] (will not match >=2 of the IDE paths usually)
  • Bot commits (Renovate/Dependabot) with skip-ci that touch tasks.json
  • Developer rebasing old branches with preserved author timestamps
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the actor account from the audit event, check its recent activity for token regeneration / SSH key additions / new OAuth grants; correlate against the May 19 PyPI durabletask incident actor. Step 2 — Contain: suspend the GitHub account, revoke all PATs and OAuth grants, force-rotate any GitHub App / Action secrets the account had access to, and revert the commit from any affected default branches. Step 3 — Hunt: GitHub code-search the org for any other repos containing the five planted paths or the commit message 'Switched DataConverter to OrchestrationContext'; query GitHub Audit Log for the same actor across all owned orgs for [skip ci] commits adding files outside src trees.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "GitHub"
| where ActionType in ("Repositories.Push","RepositoriesPush","git.push")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has "[skip ci]"
| where Raw has_any (".claude/settings.json",".gemini/settings.json",".cursor/rules/setup.mdc",".vscode/tasks.json",".github/setup.js")
| extend AuthorDate = extract(@"author[^\d]+(\d{4})-\d{2}-\d{2}", 1, Raw)
| where isnotempty(AuthorDate) and toint(AuthorDate) < 2024
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ObjectName, AuthorDate, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
// Requires GitHub Audit Log connector (GitHubAuditLogPolling_CL) or CommonSecurityLog ingest
GitHubAuditLogPolling_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where action_s == "git.push" or action_s == "repo.push"
| where commits_s has "[skip ci]"
| where commits_s has_any (".claude/settings.json",".gemini/settings.json",".cursor/rules/setup.mdc",".vscode/tasks.json",".github/setup.js")
| extend AuthorYear = extract(@"author[^\d]+(\d{4})-\d{2}-\d{2}", 1, commits_s)
| where isnotempty(AuthorYear) and toint(AuthorYear) < 2024
| project TimeGenerated, actor_s, actor_ip_s, repo_s, commits_s, AuthorYear
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:github @evt.name:git.push @commits.message:*"[skip ci]"* (@commits.added:(*.claude/settings.json* OR *.gemini/settings.json* OR *.cursor/rules/setup.mdc* OR *.vscode/tasks.json* OR *.github/setup.js*))
CLOUD
`github_audit` action=git.push | spath input=raw_event | search commits{}.message="*[skip ci]*" (commits{}.added{}="*.claude/settings.json" OR commits{}.added{}="*.gemini/settings.json" OR commits{}.added{}="*.cursor/rules/setup.mdc" OR commits{}.added{}="*.vscode/tasks.json" OR commits{}.added{}="*.github/setup.js") | eval author_year=substr('commits{}.timestamp',1,4) | where author_year<"2024" | table _time repo actor commits{}.id commits{}.message commits{}.added{} author_year
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
